title: Real-time Updates
subtitle: How to push changes to users the moment they happen — polling, long polling, SSE, WebSockets and the pub/sub layer behind them.
seoTitle: Design Real-time Updates | System Design Interview Breakdown
description: How to push changes to users the moment they happen — polling, long polling, SSE, WebSockets and the pub/sub layer behind them.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.text: Chat messages, live scores, collaborative cursors, ride locations, stock prices — a huge share of interview questions need the server to tell clients about something *as it happens*. HTTP was built for the client to ask and the server to answer, so real-time updates require deliberate design on two hops: **server → client** (how the update reaches the device) and **source → server** (how the server holding the connection learns about the update).
The Problem
Imagine a chat app. Alice sends a message; it lands on server A. Bob is connected to server B. Two things must happen:

items: Server B must find out a message for Bob exists.
Server B must deliver it to Bob's device without Bob asking.

blocks.text: Most candidates only think about the second hop. Interviewers are usually more interested in the first.

blocks.caption: The two hops of real-time delivery

blocks.text: The Solution
Hop 2: getting updates to the client

approach.text: The client asks "anything new?" every few seconds.

challenges.text: Most requests return nothing, so it wastes server capacity, and updates are delayed by up to the poll interval. It is, however, dead simple and works everywhere — a perfectly good answer when updates are infrequent and a few seconds of delay is fine.

approach.text: The client makes a request that the server holds open until there is something to send (or a timeout, say 30s). On response, the client immediately reconnects.

challenges.text: Near-real-time with plain HTTP, but each message costs a full request cycle, and bursts of updates cause reconnect storms.

approach.text: A single long-lived HTTP response streams events from server to client. Browsers reconnect automatically and resume using `Last-Event-ID`.

challenges.text: One-directional only — clients still send data with normal requests, which is exactly right for feeds, notifications, live comments and LLM token streaming. Some proxies buffer responses and need configuration.

approach.text: A persistent, bidirectional connection over TCP. Ideal when the client sends frequent messages too: chat, multiplayer games, collaborative editing.

challenges.text: Stateful connections complicate load balancing and deploys (draining connections), and you must implement heartbeats and reconnection yourself.

blocks.text: Default to SSE when updates flow mostly from server to client, and WebSockets when both sides talk constantly. Say *why* in the interview — the choice signals that you understand the traffic pattern.
Hop 1: getting updates to the right server
With millions of connections spread across many servers, the server holding a user's connection must learn about events produced elsewhere.

approach.text: Each connection server queries for new data for its users.

challenges.text: Load grows with connections × poll rate, and latency is bounded by the interval.

blocks.title: Consistent hashing of users to servers

approach.text: Route each user (or each chat room / document) to a deterministic server, so producers know exactly where to send updates.

challenges.text: Rebalancing on scale-up and failures moves connections, and a hot room can overload one server.

approach.text: Connection servers subscribe to channels for the users or topics their clients care about (Redis Pub/Sub, NATS, or Kafka for durable streams). Producers publish to the channel; the broker delivers to whichever servers are subscribed.

challenges.text: Plain pub/sub is fire-and-forget; if a client is offline the message is missed, so pair it with durable storage (an inbox) that clients sync from on reconnect.

blocks.text: When to Use in Interviews
Reach for this pattern whenever a requirement says "see changes in real time", "live", or "instantly":

items: [WhatsApp](/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/whatsapp) — WebSockets plus pub/sub between chat servers.
[FB Live Comments](/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/fb-live-comments) — SSE fan-out to many viewers.

blocks.text: Common Deep Dives
How do you handle reconnects without losing messages?

Make delivery recoverable: persist messages durably, give each a sequence number or timestamp, and have clients resync from their last seen position when they reconnect. Real-time push is the fast path; the durable store is the source of truth.
How do you load balance persistent connections?

Use a layer-4 load balancer or a connection gateway, track connections per server, and scale on connection count rather than CPU. During deploys, drain connections gradually and let clients reconnect with jittered backoff to avoid thundering herds.
What about a single topic with millions of subscribers?

Fan out hierarchically: the broker delivers to connection servers (not to individual users), and each server pushes to its own clients. Coalesce or sample updates — nobody can read 10,000 comments a second.
Conclusion

Separate the two hops. Pick the client protocol from the traffic shape (poll → long poll → SSE → WebSocket), then design how events reach the server holding the connection — usually pub/sub backed by durable storage for recovery.

quiz.question: Which protocol best fits one-way server-to-client streams such as live comments?
quiz.explanation: SSE streams events over one HTTP response and reconnects automatically.

quiz.question: What problem does pub/sub solve in a real-time system?
options: Getting an event to whichever server holds the recipient's connection
quiz.explanation: Servers subscribe to the channels their clients care about; producers publish without knowing where clients are.

quiz.question: Why pair pub/sub with durable storage?
options: Fire-and-forget delivery misses offline clients, who need to resync
quiz.explanation: Clients recover missed updates from the store on reconnect.

quiz.question: When is simple polling an acceptable answer?
options: When updates are infrequent and a few seconds of delay is fine
quiz.explanation: Polling is simple and robust when latency requirements are loose.
